arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Mogin stated the core issue is whether issuing a license counts as parting with property.
Mr. Dreeben asserted that a video poker license is property for both the state and the licensee.
Mr. Dreeben claimed the side that brought the case's scheme violates both clauses of the mail fraud statute.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the federal mail fraud statute. It asks if government-issued licenses qualify as property for fraud purposes.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the conviction overturned because issuing a license is not parting with property.
The government wants the conviction upheld because a license is property in both hands.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Mr. Mogin argues that a state does not part with property when it issues a license.
Mr. Dreeben argues that a video poker license is property for both the state and the licensee.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the reach of federal fraud laws. It determines whether government licenses trigger federal criminal jurisdiction. The outcome shapes how prosecutors charge fraud involving state-issued permits.
